subject: Islamic Studies
board: Edexcel International GCSE Islamic Studies-style course
source: Drive: Islamic Studies schemes folder - Edexcel International GCSE Islamic Studies Specification (4IS1) and 'Islamic Studies KS4 SOW' used for content areas 1.8, 1.9, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and Appendix 5 passages (33:9, 5:3, 112:1-4, 9:128-129, 4:163); assumes Year 11 pupils have already covered spec 1.1-1.7 in Year 10; RE folder checked (KS3 material only)

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Badr: reasons, events and importance
objectives: Explain why the Prophet fought the Battle of Badr
Describe the main events and outcome
Evaluate the importance of Badr for the establishment of Islam

keywords.def: the first major battle between the Muslims and Quraysh, 17 Ramadan 2 AH
criterion: Badr is called Yawm al-Furqan, the Day of Criterion
a military expedition led personally by the Prophet
payment for the release of prisoners

starter: Define Hijrah and state the year it took place.
Name two groups in Madinah after the Hijrah.
Why was the Qur'an revealed gradually?

teach.heading: Why Badr?
bullets: Muslims had lost homes and property in Makkah
Permission to fight those who wronged them was given (22:39-40)
A Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan travelled near Madinah
The caravan escaped but Quraysh sent an army
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8b: reasons the Prophet chose to fight. Present the Qur'anic permission 22:39-40 and the context of persecution and confiscated property. Misconception: the Muslims set out to attack a peaceful city; they set out to intercept a caravan and the situation changed (8:7). Ask: what is the difference between defensive and aggressive war?

teach.heading: The battle
bullets: About 313 Muslims against about 1,000 Quraysh
The Prophet prayed through the night for help
Allah promised reinforcement (3:123-125; 8:9)
Muslims won; around 70 Quraysh killed and 70 captured; 14 Muslims martyred
teach.note: State that figures are those commonly reported. Highlight Abu Jahl's death. Ask pupils to calculate the proportion: about 1 Muslim to 3 Quraysh. Link to 33:9 for the pattern of Allah's help in battles (Edexcel passage: 'remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came').

teach.heading: The prisoners
bullets: Prisoners were treated humanely
Most were freed on ransom
Reports mention literate prisoners taught Muslims to read
Allah praises feeding the captive (76:8)
teach.note: Use 'reports state'. The Prophet advised kindness to prisoners (Bukhari: he told Companions to treat them well, per Abu Aziz's narration in the seerah). Compare with ancient norms of killing or enslaving. Ask: what does this show about Islamic ethics in war?

teach.heading: Importance for Islam
bullets: The first great victory increased Muslim confidence
Raised the Muslims' standing among Arab tribes
Showed that faith and trust could overcome numbers
Led Quraysh to seek revenge at Uhud
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Develop 'establishment of Islam': political security for Madinah, morale, and tribal respect. Ask for a counter-argument: was Badr more important than Hudaybiyyah? Prepare for 12-mark.

teach.heading: Exam skill
bullets: Reasons: persecution, confiscation, protection of Madinah
Events: numbers, du'a, help of angels
Result: victory, prisoners, ransom
Importance: morale, status, security
teach.note: Create a four-box planner. Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of Badr was important to the early Muslim community.' Pupils write first reason in PEEL.

practice: Give two reasons why the Muslims fought at Badr.
What does 'Furqan' mean?
Short answer: 'State two ways the prisoners of Badr were treated' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on the importance of Badr.
Create a table of reasons, events, outcome and importance.
Plan a 12-mark answer: 'Badr was the most important battle in the life of the Prophet. Discuss.'
exit: When did Badr take place?
Give one importance of the battle.
lessons.homework: Draft the 12-mark answer; revisit it after Uhud.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: four-box planner with sentence starters; stretch: assess whether Badr was a political, military or religious turning point.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Uhud: lessons of obedience and patience
objectives: Describe the events of Uhud
Explain why the Muslims initially prevailed and then suffered setbacks
Evaluate the importance of the lessons of Uhud

keywords.def: the battle fought in Shawwal 3 AH near Mount Uhud
the Quraysh cavalry commander at Uhud, later a Muslim general
the Prophet's uncle who was martyred at Uhud

starter: Give two reasons for Badr.
What was the result of Badr?
Who commanded Quraysh at Badr?

teach.heading: The build-up
bullets: Quraysh marched with about 3,000 men for revenge
About 700 Muslims went out; 300 hypocrites withdrew
The Prophet placed 50 archers on the hill and ordered them to stay
'Do not leave your position, even if you see us seized by birds' (Bukhari)
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The consultation: some wanted to meet them outside Madinah; the Prophet agreed to go out. Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with his men. The archer's command is narrated by al-Bara' in Bukhari. Ask: why was the hill vital?

teach.heading: The turning point
bullets: Muslims initially forced the Quraysh back
Many archers left to collect spoils
Khalid ibn al-Walid attacked from behind
A rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed
teach.note: Bukhari narrates that the archers disputed; some remained with Abdullah ibn Jubayr, who was killed. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was martyred, causing the rumour. Qur'an 3:152-153 addresses this: 'Allah fulfilled His promise ... until you lost courage and disputed about the order ...'

teach.heading: Casualties and the Prophet's injuries
bullets: About 70 Muslims martyred including Hamzah and Mus'ab
The Prophet was wounded in the face and lost a tooth
Companions such as Talhah shielded him
Quraysh withdrew but did not capture Madinah
teach.note: From Bukhari and Muslim. Handle with care. Ask: what does his determination to carry on show? Mention the Muslims pursued Quraysh at Hamra al-Asad the next day to show strength (3:172-173).

teach.heading: Lessons from Uhud
bullets: Obedience to the leader is essential
Love of worldly gain can undermine faith
Hardships are tests (3:140-142)
Muhammad is a messenger; Muslims worship Allah, not a man (3:144)
teach.note: Link 3:144 to Abu Bakr's speech at the Prophet's death (a later lesson). Ask: how does losing a battle strengthen faith in the long run? Distinguish between divine promise and human conditions.

teach.heading: Comparison with Badr
bullets: Badr: victory with trust and discipline
Uhud: setback after disobedience
Both teach reliance on Allah and obedience
Both shaped the Muslim community
teach.note: Set up a comparison table. Prepare the 12-mark: 'Uhud was more important than Badr in the development of the early Muslim community. Discuss.' Pupils plan their arguments.

practice: Why were the archers important?
Describe what Khalid ibn al-Walid did.
Short answer: 'State two lessons from Uhud' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Muslims suffered losses at Uhud.'
Create a comparison chart of Badr and Uhud.
Write the opening and conclusion of a 12-mark answer on Uhud's importance.
exit: Who commanded the archers?
Give one lesson of Uhud.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer using 3:152 or 3:144 as evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: map of the battlefield with arrows; stretch: assess whether disobedience or ambition was the key cause of the setback.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of the Trench (Qur'an 33:9)
objectives: Describe the siege of Madinah and the digging of the trench
Analyse Qur'an 33:9
Explain the importance of the battle

keywords.def: the trench dug to defend Madinah
the Companion who suggested the trench
surrounding a place to cut it off

starter: Give two causes of the Muslims' losses at Uhud.
Why was the Quraysh army at Uhud larger than at Badr?
Define 'obedience'.

teach.heading: The threat
bullets: In 5 AH Quraysh and allied tribes formed a confederacy of about 10,000
The Muslims numbered about 3,000
Madinah lacked natural defences on the north
Salman suggested a trench
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8: the Trench is one of four named battles. Explain the Jewish tribe Banu Nadir's role in rallying the Ahzab after being expelled (4 AH) for plotting against the Prophet. Note this is the seerah account; present factually.

teach.heading: Digging the trench
bullets: The Prophet worked alongside the Companions
They were hungry; some tied stones on their stomachs
A hard rock was struck by the Prophet and broke
Allah gave them hope in hardship
teach.note: Bukhari (Jabir and al-Bara') records the digging, hunger, and the rock. The tying of stones is reported in Tirmidhi and others; Jabir's hadith in Bukhari tells of the small meal that fed many. Ask: how did the Prophet share their hardship?

teach.heading: The siege
bullets: The enemy could not cross the trench
Banu Qurayzah's breach of agreement increased the danger
Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud caused mistrust among the enemy
A bitter storm shattered their camp
teach.note: Qur'an 33:9 (Edexcel passage): 'O you who believe, remember Allah's favour upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see.' Annotate: favour, armies, wind, unseen armies. Treat the Banu Qurayzah aftermath factually: the treaty breach led to a siege and a judgement by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh according to their own law (Bukhari, Muslim). Be prepared to answer questions with sensitivity and sources.

teach.heading: Outcome and importance
bullets: The confederates withdrew
The Prophet said: 'Now we will march against them; they will not march against us' (Bukhari)
Madinah's security was established
Strengthened the Muslims' standing
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Ask: why was this a turning point? Compare 33:9 with Allah's help at Badr. Link to hypocrisy: the hypocrites expressed doubts (33:12-13).

teach.heading: Analysing 33:9
bullets: What does it ask believers to remember?
What did Allah send?
How does it show Allah's power?
What lesson does it give about trust?
teach.note: Model annotation and a 12-mark plan: 'The Battle of the Trench shows that victory comes only through the help of Allah. Discuss.' Include human effort (trench), unity, and divine help.

practice: Why was the trench a good idea?
Identify two parts of Allah's help in 33:9.
Short answer: 'State two details of the siege' (2 marks).
independent: Annotate 33:9 and write three comprehension answers.
Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of the Trench was important.'
Plan the 12-mark answer on divine help and human effort.
exit: Who suggested the trench?
What did Allah send upon the enemy in 33:9?
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer using 33:9 as evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diagram of Madinah and the trench; stretch: evaluate the role of strategy, morale and divine help.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Khaybar
objectives: Explain the reasons for the expedition to Khaybar
Describe the events and the settlement
Evaluate its importance

keywords.def: a fortified oasis north of Madinah, attacked in 7 AH
the Companion given the flag at Khaybar
tax paid by non-Muslim subjects in return for protection

starter: What did the Prophet say after the Trench?
Name the Companion who suggested the trench.
State one lesson from Uhud.

teach.heading: Background
bullets: After Hudaybiyyah the Muslims turned to the north
Khaybar was a base of tribes hostile to Madinah
Banu Nadir had settled there and helped incite the Ahzab
The Prophet marched in Muharram 7 AH
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8b: the reasons. Ask pupils to identify the security dimension: removing a threat to Madinah. Mention the numbers: around 1,400-1,600 Muslims. Note that sources differ on small details.

teach.heading: The campaign
bullets: The Muslims besieged the fortresses one by one
Ali was given the flag after the Prophet said: 'I will give the flag to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger'
Ali defeated the champion Marhab
The strongest forts fell
teach.note: The flag hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim (Sahl ibn Sa'd). Ali had sore eyes and the Prophet applied his saliva, and he recovered. Ask: what qualities are praised in the hadith? Avoid exaggerated stories; keep to sources.

teach.heading: The settlement
bullets: The inhabitants surrendered
They were allowed to remain and farm the land
They gave half the produce
The Prophet later sent an assessor to estimate the share
teach.note: From Bukhari and Muslim (Ibn Umar). Ask: why would the Prophet leave them on the land? (They knew farming; the Muslims had few farmers.) Mention that after Khaybar a poisoned meal was offered to the Prophet (Bukhari, Anas); he did not eat from it fully.

teach.heading: Importance of Khaybar
bullets: Removed a northern threat to Madinah
Brought economic resources
Showed Muslim strength after Hudaybiyyah
Prepared the ground for later expansion
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Compare Khaybar with the Trench: from defence to securing borders. Ask: how do you decide which battle was most important? Build criteria: security, morale, economy, spread of Islam.

teach.heading: Evaluating the four battles
bullets: Badr: first victory
Uhud: lessons of obedience
Trench: defence of Madinah
Khaybar: removing a threat
teach.note: Use a ranking diamond. Pupils justify their chosen most important battle. Prepare the 12-mark stem: 'The Battle of Badr was more important than the other battles. Discuss.'

practice: Give two reasons for the expedition to Khaybar.
What arrangement was made after the surrender?
Short answer: 'State two ways Khaybar helped Muslims' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of Khaybar was important.'
Complete a ranking diamond of the four battles with reasons.
Plan the 12-mark answer on the importance of Badr compared with others.
exit: In which year did the expedition to Khaybar take place?
Give one importance of the expedition.
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer comparing Badr with the other battles.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: comparison table with sentence stems; stretch: weigh the importance of military versus political outcomes.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 Why did the Prophet fight? Rules and ethics of war
objectives: Explain the reasons the Prophet chose to fight
Describe the rules of conduct in war
Evaluate the claim that the battles were defensive

keywords.def: striving in the way of Allah, including self-struggle and, when needed, lawful defence
going beyond the limits set by Allah

starter: Name the four battles in order.
Which battle involved a trench?
Who was given the flag at Khaybar?

teach.heading: Reasons for fighting
bullets: Persecution and expulsion from Makkah
Self-defence of the community
Protection of allies and treaties
Removal of threats to Madinah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Use 22:39-40 and 2:190. Ask pupils to find each reason in the four battles. Edexcel 1.8b requires explanation, not just listing.

teach.heading: Limits and rules
bullets: 'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress' (2:190)
Do not kill women, children or the elderly (Bukhari, Muslim)
Do not mutilate or betray
Incline to peace if the enemy inclines to it (8:61)
teach.note: The Prophet forbade killing women and children (Ibn Umar in Bukhari and Muslim). Muslim also reports his instructions to commanders to avoid treachery, mutilation and killing children. Ask: how do these rules compare with modern rules of war?

teach.heading: Treatment of the enemy
bullets: Prisoners were treated well
Agreements were honoured
Forgiveness after victory (Makkah)
Peace treaties such as Hudaybiyyah
teach.note: Link to previous lessons. Ask pupils to give an example for each principle. Misconception: the Prophet fought to force people to accept Islam. Respond with 2:256 ('There is no compulsion in religion').

teach.heading: Evaluating the claim
bullets: Argument for: each was a response to attack or threat
Argument against: Khaybar and later expeditions were pre-emptive
Scholars give security and justice as reasons
Judgement needs evidence
teach.note: Model both sides. Include different viewpoints (Muslim historians and non-Muslim historians). Encourage pupils to use phrases like 'Some argue ... others claim ...'. Provide evidence for each.

teach.heading: Exam practice
bullets: 6 marks: explain two reasons the Prophet chose to fight
12 marks: evaluate whether the battles show the Prophet's concern for justice and peace
teach.note: Plan together; pupils write the 6-mark answer. Remind them to use specific battles and sources.

practice: List three reasons the Prophet fought.
State two rules of conduct from the lesson.
Short answer: 'Explain what 2:190 teaches about fighting' (4 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Prophet chose to fight battles.'
Plan and draft the 12-mark answer on justice and peace.
Create a poster showing rules of war in Islam with sources.
exit: What does 2:190 say about transgression?
Name one rule of conduct in war.
lessons.homework: Finish the 12-mark answer; include 2:190, 8:61 and an example.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: two-column for/against grid; stretch: analyse differences between modern and classical concepts of just war.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - The final years and achievements (spec 1.9)
lessons.title: 1.9 The final pilgrimage and the Farewell Sermon (Qur'an 5:3)
objectives: Describe the Prophet's final pilgrimage
Outline the main themes of the Farewell Sermon
Analyse Qur'an 5:3

keywords.def: the plain where the sermon was delivered

starter: Name one rule of war from the Prophet.
Which battle was fought in 3 AH?
What does 2:190 say about fighting?

teach.heading: The last Hajj
bullets: In 10 AH the Prophet led the pilgrimage
A great multitude joined him
He taught the rites: 'Take your rites from me'
He stood at Arafat and delivered his sermon
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Jabir's account is in Sahih Muslim. Explain that this pilgrimage became the model for all later Hajj. Ask: why is it called the Farewell Pilgrimage?

teach.heading: The sermon: sanctity of life and wealth
bullets: Blood and property are sacred
Pre-Islamic blood feuds are abolished
Riba of the days of ignorance is abolished
Everyone is accountable to Allah
teach.note: From Muslim (Jabir). Link to human rights teaching in 1.6. Ask: why does the Prophet emphasise life and wealth first? (Foundation of justice.)

teach.heading: The sermon: equality and women
bullets: All people are from Adam; no Arab over non-Arab except by taqwa
Fear Allah concerning women
Hold fast to the Book of Allah
'Have I conveyed the message?'
teach.note: The Arab/non-Arab wording is in Ahmad (graded authentic). The Prophet ﷺ asked the crowd and they affirmed; he said 'O Allah, bear witness'. Ask: how do these themes support social justice?

teach.heading: Qur'an 5:3
bullets: Prohibited foods are listed
'This day I have perfected your religion for you'
'Completed My favour upon you'
'And approved Islam as your religion'
teach.note: Edexcel 1.9 passage. According to Bukhari, a Jewish man told Umar that if this verse had been revealed to them they would have taken that day as a festival; Umar replied that they knew where and when it was revealed: Arafat on a Friday. Discuss the meaning: the religion's essential teachings were complete.

teach.heading: Exam practice
bullets: 6 marks: explain two themes of the sermon
12 marks: 'The Farewell Sermon is the most important speech in Islamic history. Discuss.'
teach.note: Plan the 12-mark: for (summary of Islam, human rights), against (other sermons or events). Use 5:3 to anchor. Ask pupils to apply their evidence.

practice: List four themes of the Farewell Sermon.
Explain what 'perfected' means in 5:3.
Short answer: 'State two rights mentioned in the sermon' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on two themes of the sermon.
Annotate 5:3 and write a summary.
Plan and write the 12-mark answer.
exit: Where was the sermon delivered?
Quote or paraphrase a line from 5:3.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer on the Farewell Sermon.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sermon points on cards; stretch: compare the sermon with a modern human-rights document respectfully.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - The final years and achievements (spec 1.9)
lessons.title: 1.9 The Prophet's achievements and his death in Madinah
objectives: Outline the Prophet's achievements in society, religion and politics
Describe the events at his death
Evaluate his greatest achievement

keywords.def: the Highest Companion: his final words in Bukhari
what is left behind after death

starter: Name two themes of the Farewell Sermon.
Which verse says the religion was perfected?
Where was the sermon given?

teach.heading: Achievements in religion
bullets: Delivered the Qur'an
Established prayer, zakah, fasting and Hajj
Established Tawhid and ended idol worship in Arabia
Taught moral values and the Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.9c. Ask pupils to list achievements and decide which category they belong in. Remind them of the example of Makkah's idols being removed.

teach.heading: Achievements in society
bullets: Brotherhood of Muhajirun and Ansar
Rights of women, orphans and the poor
Justice and equality before the law
Abolished tribal feuds
teach.note: Link to previous teaching about equality. Give evidence from the sermon and Madinah. Ask: how did the Prophet change the attitude to the weak?

teach.heading: Achievements in politics
bullets: Founded the Madinah community and agreements
Made treaties such as Hudaybiyyah
Sent letters to rulers
United Arabia under Islam
teach.note: Explain that the Prophet corresponded with the leaders of Byzantium, Persia, Abyssinia and Egypt, as in the seerah. Ask pupils to consider leadership qualities.

teach.heading: His death
bullets: He became ill in 11 AH
He asked to be cared for in Aisha's house
Abu Bakr led the prayer during his illness
He died on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH
teach.note: Bukhari narrates that he said 'with the highest companion' (ar-Rafiq al-A'la) before passing, in Aisha's arms. Be sensitive. Ask: what does his final concern for prayer teach? Mention that Abu Bakr was appointed to lead the prayer.

teach.heading: The community's reaction
bullets: Umar could not accept the news at first
Abu Bakr said: 'Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living and never dies'
He recited 3:144
The community chose Abu Bakr as caliph
teach.note: From Bukhari. Ask: how does 3:144 protect Tawhid even after the Prophet? This links to the Tawhid unit. Prepare the 12-mark: 'The Prophet's greatest achievement was in religion, not politics. Discuss.'

practice: Sort achievements into religion, society and politics.
Describe the events at the Prophet's death.
Short answer: 'State two achievements of the Prophet' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two achievements of the Prophet in society.'
Plan and write the 12-mark answer.
Create a one-page revision sheet for Section A, 1.9.
exit: What did Abu Bakr recite after the Prophet's death?
Give one achievement in each category.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sorting cards for achievements; stretch: evaluate how religious, social and political achievements are connected.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Section B - Beliefs: Tawhid and Allah (spec 2.1)
lessons.title: 2.1 The nature of belief in Allah: Tawhid (Qur'an 112:1-4)
objectives: Explain the meaning and importance of Tawhid
Analyse Surah al-Ikhlas
Explain the three categories of Tawhid according to ahl as-sunnah
starter: State what 'Seal of the Prophets' means.
Recite or write 112:1-4.
Give the meaning of Tawhid.

teach.heading: Surah al-Ikhlas
bullets: 'Say: He is Allah, One'
'Allah, the Eternal Refuge'
'He neither begets nor is begotten'
'And there is none comparable to Him'
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.1 passage. Annotate each ayah: unity, independence, no parents or children, uniqueness. Also mention the Prophet's statement that it equals a third of the Qur'an (Bukhari).

teach.heading: Meaning and importance
bullets: The foundation of Islam: La ilaha illa Allah
All prophets called to it (21:25)
It shapes worship, trust and character
It is the basis for salvation
teach.note: Ask: if you believe in one Creator, how does that change your relationship with the world? Link to the Sunni understanding of Tawhid as a lived reality, not just a statement.

teach.heading: Three categories
bullets: Rububiyyah: Allah alone is Lord, Creator and Sustainer
Uluhiyyah: Allah alone is worshipped
Asma wa Sifat: Allah's names and attributes are unique and perfect
No likening, no denial
teach.note: This is how ahl as-sunnah classify Tawhid based on the Qur'an and Sunnah. Examples: 39:62 (Rububiyyah), 1:5 (Uluhiyyah), 42:11 (Names and attributes). Pupils produce a chart with example.

teach.heading: Characteristics of Allah in the Qur'an
bullets: Al-Hayy, Al-Qayyum (2:255)
Al-Alim, the All-Knowing
Al-Aziz, Al-Hakim
Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim
teach.note: Edexcel 2.1d. Read Ayat al-Kursi in English. Ask pupils to extract characteristics. Link each to belief and behaviour.

teach.heading: Exam skills
bullets: Define Tawhid in one sentence
Use 112 to support your explanation
Show how belief in Tawhid affects life
teach.note: Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two ways in which Surah al-Ikhlas teaches Tawhid.' Pupils write first point. Discuss 12-mark stem: 'Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam. Discuss.'

practice: Write the meaning of each ayah of Surah al-Ikhlas.
State one example of each category of Tawhid.
Short answer: 'Explain what 'As-Samad' means' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on how 112 teaches Tawhid.
Create a chart of the three categories with verses.
Plan the 12-mark answer on Tawhid being the most important belief.
exit: Define Tawhid.
What does 'Ahad' mean?
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer on Tawhid with evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: ayah-by-ayah meaning cards; stretch: explain how Surah al-Ikhlas answers different false beliefs.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Section B - Beliefs: Tawhid and Allah (spec 2.1)
lessons.title: 2.1 The attributes of Allah: omnipotence, Creator, Merciful and Just
objectives: Explain Allah's omnipotence, creatorship, mercy and justice
Use Qur'anic evidence to support explanations
Evaluate how the attributes balance each other

keywords.def: the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

starter: List the three categories of Tawhid.
Which category does 1:5 relate to?
Define Ahad.

teach.heading: Omnipotence
bullets: 'Allah is over all things Competent' (2:20)
'Be, and it is' (36:82)
Nothing is beyond His power
Belief inspires trust and humility
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: how does belief in an All-Powerful Creator change fear and hope? Explain tawakkul. Edexcel 2.1b: omnipotence.

teach.heading: Creator
bullets: Allah created the heavens, earth and humans
'Allah is Creator of all things' (39:62)
Creation shows His wisdom and power (3:190)
We are accountable as His servants
teach.note: Ask pupils for examples of signs of creation. Connect to gratitude and responsibility as khalifah. Note that creation implies ownership and care.

teach.heading: Merciful
bullets: 'My mercy encompasses all things' (7:156)
Prophet: 'My mercy overcomes My anger' (Bukhari, Muslim)
Every surah but one begins with bismillah
Hope and repentance
teach.note: Mention the hadith of the mother and child (Bukhari, Muslim), in which the Prophet said Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child. Ask: how does mercy motivate good deeds?

teach.heading: Just
bullets: 'Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight' (4:40)
Every deed is weighed (21:47)
Justice requires accountability
Allah's justice and mercy work together
teach.note: Discuss how mercy and justice balance: hope and fear. Misconception: justice means no mercy. Correct with the hadith that Allah's mercy has a hundred parts (Muslim). Prepare the 12-mark stem: 'Allah's mercy is more important than His justice. Discuss.'

teach.heading: Putting attributes into practice
bullets: Trust Allah in difficulty
Be merciful and just to others
Seek forgiveness
Worship with love and fear
teach.note: Pupils plan how each attribute affects behaviour. Exam link: use specific attributes with examples from the Qur'an.

practice: Match each attribute with its verse.
Explain how mercy and justice complement each other.
Short answer: 'State two things that show Allah as Creator' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two attributes of Allah and their importance for Muslims.'
Draft the 12-mark answer on mercy and justice.
Create a table of attributes, evidence and effect on behaviour.
exit: Name two attributes of Allah.
Give one effect belief in His mercy has.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer; include a different viewpoint and a conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: attribute cards with verses; stretch: discuss how Muslims avoid both despair and presumption.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Section B - Beliefs: Tawhid and Allah (spec 2.1)
lessons.title: 2.1 Shirk and nifaq (hypocrisy)
objectives: Define shirk and nifaq
Explain why they are condemned
Analyse examples and consequences

keywords.def: hypocrisy: outwardly showing faith while hiding disbelief or insincerity

starter: Define Tawhid.
Name one attribute of Allah.
What does 112:4 teach?

teach.heading: Shirk
bullets: 'Allah does not forgive that partners be set up with Him' (4:48)
'Shirk is a great injustice' (31:13)
Greatest sin: making a rival to Allah (Bukhari, Muslim)
Includes idols, worship of the self, and giving Allah's rights to others
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain 4:48: Allah does not forgive dying upon shirk, but forgives less for whom He wills; repentance before death is accepted. Edexcel 2.1c. Examples: idolatry; asking the dead to remove harm. Pupils define major and minor.

teach.heading: Minor shirk and riya
bullets: Showing off in worship
Seeking praise from people
Swearing by other than Allah
Reliance on omens
teach.note: Scholars consider these minor shirk and grave sins; riya can nullify the reward of a deed. Link to the hadith of intentions. Ask: how can a teenager guard against riya on social media?

teach.heading: Nifaq: hypocrisy
bullets: The munafiqun professed faith but hid disbelief (63:1-3)
'The hypocrites are in the lowest depths of the Fire' (4:145)
Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew at Uhud
Nifaq in deeds: lying, breaking promises, betraying trust
teach.note: Distinguish major nifaq (belief) from minor (actions). Hadith: three signs of the hypocrite (Bukhari, Muslim). Remind pupils that only Allah knows hearts and we do not accuse individuals.

teach.heading: Consequences
bullets: Loss of reward in the Hereafter
Division and harm to the community
Spiritual emptiness
Repentance is always open (4:146)
teach.note: Highlight the exception in 4:146: those who repent, reform and hold fast to Allah. Ask: how does Islam combine warnings with hope?

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Explain what shirk and nifaq mean
Give Qur'anic evidence
Explain why each is condemned
teach.note: Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why shirk is the greatest sin in Islam.' Plan the 12-mark: 'Nifaq is as dangerous to the Muslim community as shirk. Discuss.'

practice: Define shirk and nifaq.
Give examples of major and minor shirk.
Short answer: 'State two characteristics of the hypocrites' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on why shirk is the greatest sin.
Draft the 12-mark answer on nifaq and the community.
Create a table comparing shirk and nifaq.
exit: Give a verse that condemns shirk.
Name one sign of hypocrisy.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer with a conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: definitions and example cards; stretch: analyse the difference between disbelief and sinful behaviour in nifaq.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Section B - Prophethood and revelation (spec 2.2-2.3)
lessons.title: 2.2 Risalah: the importance of prophethood and the earlier prophets (Qur'an 9:128-129)
objectives: Explain the nature and importance of prophethood
Describe the lives of Adam, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Musa, Dawud and Isa
Analyse Qur'an 9:128-129

keywords.def: protection of prophets from major sins and errors in conveying the message
a miracle given to a prophet by Allah's permission

starter: Give two attributes of Allah.
Define shirk.
Name the last prophet.

teach.heading: What is prophethood?
bullets: Prophets are chosen men who receive revelation
They convey Allah's message and show how to live
'We sent to every nation a messenger' (16:36)
They are human, not divine (18:110)
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.2a-b. Ask: why do humans need guidance? Emphasise that prophets are role models. Include belief in all prophets without distinction (2:285).

teach.heading: Adam, Ibrahim and Isma'il
bullets: Adam: first human and prophet; repented (2:37)
Ibrahim: stood for Tawhid; tested with the idols and sacrifice
Isma'il: patient son; helped build the Ka'bah
Hajj rites recall Ibrahim and family
teach.note: Keep to Qur'anic and sound accounts. Ibrahim's rejection of idols: 21:51-70; his test: 37:102-107; building of the Ka'bah: 2:127. Ask: how is Hajj linked to Ibrahim?

teach.heading: Musa, Dawud and Isa
bullets: Musa: led Bani Isra'il from Pharaoh; received the Tawrah
Dawud: king and prophet; received the Zabur
Isa: born miraculously to Maryam; received the Injil
Isa is a messenger of Allah, not divine (4:171)
teach.note: Be respectful toward Christians and Jews: Muslims honour Musa and Isa as prophets. Explain differences in belief clearly and politely. Ask: what does the Qur'an say about Isa's miracles by Allah's permission (3:49)?

teach.heading: Qur'an 9:128-129
bullets: 'There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves'
'Grievous to him is what you suffer'
'Eager for you; to the believers kind and merciful'
'Sufficient for me is Allah; on Him I rely'
teach.note: Edexcel passage. Annotate: closeness, compassion, trust. Link to the Prophet's care for his ummah (hadith: du'a 'my Ummah, my Ummah' in Muslim). Ask: what qualities of a prophet appear?

teach.heading: Importance and lessons
bullets: Prophets deliver guidance and show how to apply it
They teach patience, trust and mercy
They unify humanity under one message
Muhammad is their seal
teach.note: Prepare 6-mark: 'Explain two lessons Muslims learn from the lives of the prophets.' Pupils choose two prophets. 12-mark stem: 'The prophets are more important as role models than as messengers. Discuss.'

practice: Match each prophet to a key event or book.
State two qualities of prophets.
Short answer: 'Explain why prophets were sent' (4 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer using two prophets as examples.
Annotate 9:128-129.
Plan the 12-mark answer on prophets as role models.
exit: Name two prophets and their books.
Give one quality of the Prophet Muhammad from 9:128.
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer on role models.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: prophet timeline cards; stretch: compare how different prophets faced opposition.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Section B - Prophethood and revelation (spec 2.2-2.3)
lessons.title: 2.3 The holy books of Islam (Qur'an 4:163)
objectives: Describe the nature of the Tawrah, Zabur, Injil and Scrolls of Ibrahim
Explain the importance of the holy books in establishing Islam
Analyse Qur'an 4:163

keywords.def: guardian and criterion over earlier scriptures (5:48)

starter: Name three prophets from the previous lesson.
State the meaning of ismah.
Which verse says there is a messenger to every nation?

teach.heading: Revelation through books
bullets: Books are Allah's words given to messengers
The message was the same: worship Allah alone
The Qur'an is the final revelation
Belief in the books is a pillar of iman
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.3. Link to the hadith of Jibril. Ask: why did Allah send books as well as prophets?

teach.heading: Qur'an 4:163
bullets: 'We have revealed to you as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him'
Lists Ibrahim, Isma'il, Is'haq, Ya'qub, Isa and others
'And We gave Dawud the Zabur'
One chain of revelation
teach.note: Edexcel passage. Annotate names. Ask: what does the verse show about the unity of revelation?

teach.heading: Earlier books
bullets: Suhuf of Ibrahim
Tawrah to Musa
Zabur to Dawud
Injil to Isa
teach.note: Explain Muslim belief that these were true revelations. Muslims believe that the Qur'an corrects and confirms what is true (5:48) and that earlier texts changed over time, a view that Muslims hold respectfully. Avoid disparaging language. Ask: what does it mean for the Qur'an to be a criterion over earlier books?

teach.heading: The importance of the books
bullets: Show that Allah guides every nation
Establish Tawhid and the Day of Judgment
The Qur'an completes and confirms earlier guidance
Muslims respect the earlier prophets and their books
teach.note: Edexcel 2.3b. Pupils suggest how respect for earlier books leads to respectful relations with Jews and Christians (People of the Book, 29:46: 'do not argue except in the best way'). Ask: how can this guide interfaith conversations?

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Name each book and prophet
Explain the role of the Qur'an as final
Link to belief in prophets
teach.note: Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why Muslims believe in the earlier holy books.' 12-mark: 'The Qur'an is the only holy book Muslims need. Discuss.' Plan together and balance points on respect for earlier books and the Qur'an's finality.

practice: Match each prophet with their book.
Explain what 'muhaymin' means.
Short answer: 'State two reasons Muslims believe in earlier books' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on belief in earlier holy books.
Annotate 4:163 with the list of prophets.
Plan and write the 12-mark answer on the Qur'an as the only book needed.
exit: Name the four earlier books or scrolls.
What does 5:48 say about the Qur'an?
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer and prepare a revision sheet for 2.1-2.3.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching grid of prophets and books; stretch: evaluate how the Qur'an's finality affects interfaith relations.
